title: Agentic alert triage: simple checks first, case built before analyst opens it
problem: Manual investigation of each alert took about half an hour; Elastic's first AI summaries were wrong about 40% of the time, so analysts stopped reading them.
approach: Rule-based queries close obvious false positives; narrow agents investigate the rest and build a case with a verdict.
Only high-confidence false positives close without an analyst; analysts confirm or override and record when the AI was wrong.
Elastic reports AI verdict correctness rising from 60% to 92% after changing the context given to agents, not the models (self-reported).
Elastic reports a 30-minute investigation now finishing in under 3 minutes (self-reported).

title: Precedent retrieval showing analysts how similar alerts were closed before
problem: Many alerts resemble cases already investigated, but proving that meant digging through closed tickets, raw logs and colleagues' Slack comments.
approach: Figma indexes alerts with on-call comments, retrieves similar recent alerts, posts a summary and downgrades severity when similar alerts were benign.
Expel's precedent engine shows a suggested read and nearest past cases; weak matches default to escalation and the analyst always decides.
Figma reports a 20% drop in on-call pages (self-reported); Expel publishes targets, not measured results.

title: SIEM triage agent proposes a verdict and next steps; analyst decides
problem: Analysts pivot manually across data to gather context for every queued finding before deciding whether to close, escalate or investigate it.
approach: Google, Splunk, Microsoft and Cisco embed triage agents in the security monitoring platform (SIEM); the agent proposes a disposition and rationale.
Analysts decide whether a finding is closed, escalated or acted on; high-impact actions stay with people.
Google says a typical 30-minute analysis falls to about 60 seconds (vendor-published); Cisco's event figures are observations, not benchmarks.

title: Agent triages user-reported phishing emails and resolves false alarms
problem: User-reported suspicious emails arrive continuously; reviewing each one slows response and risks genuine threats being missed.
approach: An agent detonates files and URLs, checks threat intelligence, classifies the email and explains its verdict in plain language.
False positives are resolved; true positives stay open for an analyst, who can give feedback on the classification.
Valvoline's CISO says analysts reclaimed hours and containment became automatic on Torq's platform (vendor-published); no figures.

title: AI SOC analyst investigates every first-line alert and closes the benign majority
problem: Alert volume grew faster than analyst headcount and most alerts were benign; at Zapier a very small team faced 50-100+ daily investigations.
approach: Alerts flow from detection tools into an AI analyst that investigates each one and writes outcomes into the case system.
Analysts work only what is not closed and see every query and piece of evidence; CyberProof adds QA sampling of closed cases.
ECS reports 70% of first-line alerts closed automatically (vendor-published); Zapier reports triage falling from 10-15 minutes to under 2 (vendor-published).

title: Calibrated models score alerts; confident benign ones close, others go to analysts
problem: Noise and low-severity alerts consume analyst time, and prose-generating AI triage is costly, variable and hard to audit.
approach: Practitioners argue to start where error cost is lowest: close only alerts judged benign at a stated confidence, keeping recall fixed.
Decision models return a score with a probability: high closes, low escalates, the middle band goes to analysts, each verdict logged.
CrowdStrike reports false-positive recall rising from 21.8% to 64.8% with reasoning before the verdict (vendor-published).

title: Evidence-gated dismissal: an independent challenge must find counter-evidence before dismissal
problem: Triage agents tend to dismiss attack alerts when searches return nothing, and self-review in the same context does not correct errors.
approach: Grow Therapy's model must argue against each finding and produce counter-evidence before dismissing it; Slack uses a separate Critic agent.
Surviving findings go to analysts, who mark false positive or escalate.
Grow Therapy reports about 40% of findings were noise without the phase (self-reported); a benchmark design cut false negatives to 3.1% (independent).

title: 'SOCless' model: AI investigates all alerts, engineers paged only for serious events
problem: A small, all-senior engineering team targeted by state-sponsored attackers was swamped by thousands of monthly alerts, mostly false positives.
approach: All alert types go to an AI SOC analyst; results return to the SIEM and on-call engineers are paged for serious events.
Mysten has no dedicated security analysts.
Monthly alerts needing human review fell from thousands to under 20; time per alert from 30-60 minutes to roughly 1 (vendor-published).

title: Agent investigates alerts end to end; on-call staff supervise and correct
problem: Gathering context was the main burden for on-call engineers, and a single-prompt prototype at Slack was highly variable and sometimes jumped to spurious conclusions.
approach: Figma's agent works in the Slack alert thread with scoped tools; Slack splits investigation across Director, Expert and Critic model calls.
The on-call engineer reviews what the agent found, confirms or corrects it, and handles cases needing judgment.
Figma reports a 71% reduction in alert time to resolution (self-reported).

title: Agent prepares the investigation and the analyst decides, tested in controlled studies
problem: Manual investigations are slow, vary by analyst and degrade with fatigue, and vendors claim AI helps with little controlled evidence.
approach: Analysts receive an agent's evidence gathering and draft conclusion, review it and remain author of the verdict.
A Cloud Security Alliance study with Dropzone AI randomly assigned 148 participants; assisted analysts were 45% and 61% faster (vendor-published).
A university security team reports about 40% less ticket completion time (independent).
who: CSA, Dropzone AI, a university SOC

title: Agent-written investigation narratives help new analysts work above their experience
problem: New analysts spend their first hours learning where every tool lives and assembling context manually, and juniors take months to ramp up.
approach: Analysts start from an agent-prepared incident narrative, evidence and recommended next steps, then validate and decide.
At one customer, junior analysts learned from the agent's visible investigation reasoning.
Cabinetworks says junior ramp-up fell from months to weeks (vendor-published); Cisco Live reports a dozen-plus new analysts operating at Tier 2 level.

title: Analyst copilot and chat assistants for queries, log analysis and incident summaries
problem: Analysts take time to gather and read incident information from many sources, and most use AI individually without organisational structure or validation.
approach: A copilot in the XDR portal aggregates incident information and answers natural-language queries; the analyst remains decision-maker and author.
Microsoft authors associate copilot adoption with a 30.13% lower mean time to resolution after three months (vendor-published).
SANS reports 79% of SOCs use AI or ML tools but only 36% have built them into a defined workflow (independent).

title: Agent drafts the investigation report for analyst sign-off
problem: Analysts write structured reports for technical and non-technical readers after gathering evidence across tools, and report detail can decline with fatigue.
approach: Pan-American Life's agent produces structured reports with MITRE ATT&CK mapping, technical for analysts and plain-language for others.
Expel's Ruxie writes plain-language incident reports that people review and sign off before they are final.
CrowdStrike says Pan-American Life's reporting that once took hours now arrives automatically (vendor-published); no figures.

title: AI triage of anomaly signals surfaces an intrusion no single rule flagged
problem: Separating real signals from daily noise is hard, and rules miss activity that no single alert flags, so false negatives go unseen.
approach: Hugging Face says its anomaly-detection pipeline uses AI triage over security telemetry, and correlating those signals flagged an intrusion.
Responders handled containment and assessment; alerting was changed so a high-severity signal pages a responder within minutes.
The disclosure credits AI-assisted detection with surfacing the compromise (self-reported); no figures.

title: AI drafts, translates and scores detection rules, with judge model and review
problem: Turning each new high-severity vulnerability or threat report into a validated detection rule took research, tuning and peer review, so coverage had to be prioritised.
approach: Amazon's RuleForge scores exploit code, runs parallel rule-generation agents and uses a separate judge model to score each rule.
A security engineer reviews the best rule; human judgment is the final gate before production.
Amazon reports rules produced 336% faster and 67% fewer false positives from the judge model (self-reported).

title: Coding agents validate detections end to end in a lab, then retry
problem: Rules pass code review but nobody checks that telemetry arrives and the detection fires, and driving labs by hand is slow.
approach: DNB's Cyber Defense Center repurposed coding agents to write attack simulations, detonate them in a lab, query Splunk and rewrite on failure.
A person reviewed every generated simulation.
DNB reports most simulations were fit for purpose and the loop surfaced mechanical pipeline issues (self-reported; numbers redacted); piloting.

title: Agent drafts allowlist and rule-change proposals after analyst confirms a false positive
problem: Alerts keep firing for known-benign patterns until someone writes the suppression.
approach: When an on-call engineer confirms a false positive, Figma's agent opens a draft pull request with an allowlist entry or rule tune.
Pull requests open as drafts for human review, and the agent responds to reviewer comments.
Figma says the step from understanding an alert to a fixing pull request 'surprised us most' in time saved (self-reported); no figures.

title: SOC teams build their own agents from playbooks in a no-code workspace
problem: Each SOC has its own playbooks and escalation paths; that knowledge is lost to turnover, and generic automation does not capture it.
approach: Analysts encode playbooks and SOPs into agents in plain language on CrowdStrike's Charlotte AI AgentWorks.
For each workflow, teams set what is fully automated and what requires approval.
One analyst reports building the same agent in four minutes versus six to eight hours in Microsoft Copilot (vendor-published).

title: Agents propose containment actions that run only as validated, templated commands
problem: Blocking, killing a process or isolating a host can cause harm if the agent is wrong or manipulated, including by a single adversarial alert.
approach: Google previews agentic containment pairing agents with fixed playbooks that keep high-impact actions under analyst control.
A research design confines model output to templated commands behind an argument validator, with human approval or a delay window.
A stock guardrail proxy raised injection recall from 25.0% to 94.5% at 0.1% false positives (independent).

title: Per-action authority for SOC agents, with activity observable and stoppable
problem: AI shortened investigation but not the distance to a safe, verified response, and teams lack a shared way to decide which actions an agent may take alone.
approach: Grant authority one action at a time: the UK NCSC proposes scoring each automation on potency, scope, criticality, rollout confidence and recoverability.
The accountable owner approves each autonomy level and can widen or withdraw it; agent activity is logged, attributable and stoppable.
A vendor-run survey found 57% require a human to review every AI decision before an alert is closed (vendor-published).

title: Measuring the SOC's AI: score verdicts, sample closures, replay benchmarks
problem: Vendors give clean accuracy figures on curated alerts, but teams need evidence on their own alerts, especially false negatives.
approach: Record the AI verdict and the analyst's closure reason on every case, and sample AI-closed cases for quality review.
Before go-live and after each change, test on real alerts or replay benchmarks, and decide autonomy on the results.
Elastic reports AI-analyst agreement rising from 60% to 92% (self-reported); an independent benchmark found every approach missed at least 40.4% of attacks.

title: Managed detection services move to agent-led, human-accountable models
problem: Alerts are investigated in tiers while attackers move, buyers face a wave of 'AI MDR' products, and regulated buyers must show control over suppliers.
approach: Providers describe specialist and judge agents with a route to human experts when confidence is low; Gartner defines MDR as 'AI-augmented, human-led'.
Buyers can use the NCSC's list of AI risks as a supplier questionnaire and sign off third-party risk before onboarding.
Expel reports 14 minutes mean time to remediate on fully automated high and critical incidents (self-reported).

title: SOC staffed to build and supervise automation with coding agents
problem: Detection and response need custom automation while teams are small, and manual-triage roles are the smallest, lowest-paid and least automated family in SOC hiring.
approach: Job postings ask detection and response engineers to use AI coding tools and some ask for experience building agentic SOC workflows.
The analyst tier validates AI output.
D3 Security's sample of US SOC postings found 247 build-family versus 68 SOC analyst postings (vendor-published).

title: Idea: defender agents that contain an active attack without a human
problem: Idea, not a deployment: the field is in awe of models that find vulnerabilities while patching and detection lag, and Hugging Face's attacker was bound by no usage policy.
approach: Idea: guardrailed agents stop an active attack without human intervention; no production deployment was found.
A DARPA-derived programme planned to deploy red and blue team agents on digital twins of water systems.
No human checkpoint is defined; no results are published.
